sentences.nl: Dit is een herhalingsles.
sentences.en: This is a revision lesson.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• This is a repetition lesson.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Dit" is a demonstrative pronoun meaning "this."  
• "Is" is the third person singular form of the verb "zijn" (to be).  
• "Een" is the indefinite article "a" or "an."  
• "Herhalingsles" is a compound noun made of "herhaling" (repetition) and "les" (lesson). In Dutch, compound nouns are commonly formed by combining words without spaces.  

Extra phrases:  
• Dit is een oefening. (This is an exercise.)  
• Dit is een voorbeeld. (This is an example.)  
• Dit is een uitdaging. (This is a challenge.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Dit is een introductiecursus. (This is an introductory course.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch education, "herhalingsles" is often used to refer to lessons designed to review or consolidate previously learned material.

sentences.nl: Zij troost hem.
sentences.en: She comforts him.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• She comforts him.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Zij" is the subject pronoun for "she."  
• "Troost" is the verb in the present tense, meaning "comforts." In Dutch, the verb usually comes in the second position in a main clause.  
• "Hem" is the object pronoun for "him." Dutch uses object pronouns similarly to English.  

Extra phrases:  
• Zij helpt hem. (She helps him.)  
• Hij ziet haar. (He sees her.)  
• Wij horen jullie. (We hear you.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Zij omarmt hem. (She hugs him.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• None

sentences.nl: Marieke is echt het leukste meisje in de wereld.
sentences.en: Marieke is really the nicest girl in the world.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Marieke is really the nicest girl in the world.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Echt" means "really" and is used for emphasis. It can modify adjectives or verbs.  
• "Het leukste" is the superlative form of "leuk" (nice/fun), with "het" indicating the definite article for superlative adjectives.  
• "In de wereld" means "in the world," using the preposition "in" to denote location.

• Extra phrases:  
  - "Hij is echt de beste zanger." (He is really the best singer.)  
  - "Zij is het slimste kind in de klas." (She is the smartest child in the class.)  
  - "Dit is echt een mooie stad." (This is really a beautiful city.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Pieter is echt de grappigste jongen op school." (Pieter is really the funniest boy at school.)

sentences.nl: Als je verliefd bent,, denk je dat die persoon de enige is:, de leukste, de mooiste, de liefste…
sentences.en: When you are in love, you think that person is the only one: the nicest, the most beautiful, the sweetest…
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• If you in love are, think you that that person the only is, the nicest, the most beautiful, the sweetest...

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Als je verliefd bent" uses the subordinating conjunction "als" (if/when), which pushes the verb "bent" (are) to the end of the clause.  
• "Denk je dat" introduces a subordinate clause with "dat" (that), which also sends the verb "is" (is) to the end of the clause.  
• The sentence uses superlative adjectives: "de leukste" (the nicest), "de mooiste" (the most beautiful), "de liefste" (the sweetest).

Extra examples:  
• Als het regent, blijven we thuis. (If it rains, we stay home.)  
• Hij denkt dat het boek interessant is. (He thinks that the book is interesting.)  
• Zij is de slimste van de klas. (She is the smartest in the class.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Als je honger hebt, lijkt elk eten lekker. (If you're hungry, every food seems tasty.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch culture, being direct about feelings, such as love or admiration, is generally appreciated. However, Dutch people tend to express such emotions in a more reserved and pragmatic manner compared to some other cultures.

sentences.nl: Zo bedoelde ik het natuurlijk niet…
sentences.en: Of course, I didn't mean it that way...
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• So meant I it of course not...

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Zo" is used to mean "so" or "like this," indicating manner or way.  
• "Bedoelde" is the past tense of "bedoelen," which means "to mean" or "to intend."  
• "Het" is a pronoun meaning "it."  
• "Natuurlijk" means "of course" or "naturally," often used to emphasize understanding or agreement.  
• "Niet" is a negation word meaning "not."

• Extra Phrases:  
  - "Zo zie ik het niet." (That's not how I see it.)  
  - "Natuurlijk wil ik helpen." (Of course, I want to help.)  
  - "Ik bedoelde het anders." (I meant it differently.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Zo had ik het niet verwacht." (I didn't expect it like that.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)

sentences.nl: Ik ben nog vrijgezel.
sentences.en: I am still single.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• I am still single.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Ik ben" is the first person singular form of "zijn" (to be), used here in the present tense.  
• "Nog" means "still" and is used to indicate that a situation has not changed.  
• "Vrijgezel" is an adjective meaning "single" or "unmarried." It can also be used as a noun to mean "bachelor" or "spinster."

• Example 1: Ik ben nog bezig. (I am still busy.)  
• Example 2: Hij is nog op kantoor. (He is still at the office.)  
• Example 3: Zij is vrijgezel. (She is single.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Ik ben nog steeds aan het leren. (I am still studying.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch culture, discussing relationship status is common in casual conversation, especially among friends. It's not unusual to ask someone if they are "vrijgezel" during social gatherings.

sentences.nl: Ondertussen wordt het langzaam donker, bij het bruggetje.
sentences.en: Meanwhile, it is slowly getting dark at the little bridge.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Meanwhile becomes it slowly dark, at the little bridge.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Ondertussen" is an adverb meaning "meanwhile," often used to indicate simultaneous actions.  
• "Wordt" is the third person singular present form of "worden," meaning "to become."  
• "Het" is a definite article here, but it serves as the subject pronoun meaning "it" in this context.  
• "Langzaam" is an adverb meaning "slowly," describing the manner of becoming dark.  
• "Donker" is an adjective meaning "dark," used here as a complement in the sentence.  
• "Bij" is a preposition meaning "at" or "near."  
• "Bruggetje" is the diminutive form of "brug" (bridge), adding a nuance of smallness or endearment.

**Extra Sentences**  
• "Ondertussen kookt hij het avondeten." (Meanwhile, he cooks dinner.)  
• "Het wordt langzaam warmer buiten." (It is slowly becoming warmer outside.)  
• "We wachten bij het station." (We are waiting at the station.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Ondertussen leest zij een boek in de tuin." (Meanwhile, she is reading a book in the garden.)  

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• The use of diminutives like "bruggetje" is common in Dutch and adds a layer of affection or smallness to the noun, often used to convey familiarity or endearment.

sentences.nl: Het liefdesverdriet van Martin duurde niet zo lang.
sentences.en: Martin's heartbreak didn't last very long.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• The heartbreak of Martin lasted not so long.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Het liefdesverdriet van Martin" is a noun phrase meaning "the heartbreak of Martin," where "van" indicates possession.  
• "Duurde" is the past tense of "duren," meaning "to last."  
• "Niet zo lang" means "not so long," with "niet" as the negation and "zo lang" meaning "so long."

• Example 1: "Het huis van mijn oma is groot." (The house of my grandmother is big.)  
• Example 2: "Zijn vakantie duurde twee weken." (His vacation lasted two weeks.)  
• Example 3: "De film was niet zo spannend." (The movie was not so exciting.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Het probleem met de computer was snel opgelost." (The problem with the computer was quickly solved.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• None

nederlands.spelling: The 'ee' in 'nee' is a long vowel /eː/ and the 'a' in 'lands' is a short vowel /ɑ/.
nederlands.fast: In rapid speech, the final /ts/ in 'nederlands' may be reduced, causing it to blend with following words.

dit.spelling: The short vowel /ɪ/ is followed by a voiceless plosive /t/, typical of closed syllables.
dit.fast: In rapid speech, the /t/ in ‘dit is’ can become a flap [ɾ] or be elided entirely.

een.spelling: The article ‘een’ is pronounced with a long /eː/ to distinguish it from the numeral ‘één’, which has a stressed pronunciation.
een.fast: In rapid speech, ‘een’ may be reduced to a schwa sound /ən/ when it is unstressed.

oefenen.spelling: The sequence 'oe' represents a long /uː/ sound.
oefenen.fast: In casual speech, the final /n/ in ‘oefenen’ may be fully assimilated or nasalized before a vowel.

grammatica.spelling: The initial gr- and -a- in 'grammatica' follow the usual Dutch pronunciation rules for similar Greek-origin words.
grammatica.fast: In rapid speech, the final /a/ in 'grammatica' may be pronounced as a schwa [ə] when followed by a word starting with a consonant.

van.spelling: The short vowel /ɑ/ is common in monosyllabic words ending in -n.
van.fast: The final /n/ in ‘van’ is often elided in casual speech, particularly before consonants.

martin.spelling: The /ɑ/ in the first syllable is a short vowel due to the closed syllable pattern.
martin.fast: In connected speech, the /n/ at the end of ‘martin’ may assimilate to a nasalized vowel before a following vowel sound.

staan.spelling: The open syllable sta- lengthens vowel to /aː/.
staan.fast: The final /n/ in ‘staan’ may be elided or nasalized before a following vowel.

nog.spelling: The word 'nog' ends in a voiced velar fricative /x/, which is common in Dutch adverbs.
nog.fast: In rapid speech, the final /x/ in ‘nog’ may be devoiced or slightly reduced before a vowel.

het.spelling: The ‘h’ is often silent in casual speech, making it sound like ‘et’.
het.fast: In rapid speech, the initial /h/ in ‘het’ may be elided, resulting in a pronunciation closer to [ɛt].

bij.spelling: The diphthong /ɛi̯/ is common in Dutch, often spelled with 'ij'.
bij.fast: In fast speech, the diphthong /ɛi̯/ in 'bij' might be slightly reduced, blending smoothly into following words.

dat.spelling: Short vowel /ɑ/ in a closed syllable is represented by a single 'a'.
dat.fast: In connected speech, the /d/ in ‘dat is’ may be voiced to a soft [d̪] before the vowel.

marieke.spelling: The name Marieke features a schwa /ə/ often found in unstressed syllables.
marieke.fast: In casual speech, the final /ə/ in 'Marieke' might be less pronounced, sounding almost like a short /ə/ or even omitted.

ben.spelling: Short vowel /ɛ/ in closed syllable with nasal ending.
ben.fast: In rapid speech, 'ben ik' may sound like [bɛnɪk] with reduced vowel.

naar.spelling: The long vowel /aː/ appears in the open syllable with the consonant ending.
naar.fast: The final /r/ in ‘naar’ can often be a tapped [ɾ] or even silent in casual speech when followed by a word starting with a consonant.

die.spelling: In Dutch, the pronoun 'die' is pronounced with a long /i/ sound, which is common for pronouns and demonstratives.
die.fast: In connected speech, 'die' may become a reduced vowel sound, especially in fast speech or informal contexts.

over.spelling: The open syllable 'o-' shows the long /oː/ vowel.
over.fast: In connected speech, final /r/ in 'over' may be pronounced as a flap or even omitted depending on regional accents.

dan.spelling: Short vowel /ɑ/ in closed syllable, typical for monosyllabic adverbs.
dan.fast: In rapid speech, 'dan ik' may have the /n/ assimilated to [ŋ] before a velar sound.

heb.spelling: Heb is a monosyllabic word with a short vowel /ɛ/ followed by a voiced bilabial plosive /b/.
heb.fast: In rapid speech, the final /b/ in ‘heb ik’ might be pronounced as a flap or even omitted entirely before the following vowel.

wel.spelling: The short vowel /ɛ/ is pronounced because the syllable is closed by the consonant /l/.
wel.fast: In connected speech, the /l/ in ‘wel ik’ might become a dark [ɫ] before a vowel.

maar.spelling: The long vowel /aː/ appears in the open syllable.
maar.fast: In fast speech, the /r/ in 'maar ik' may be reduced or assimilated to the following vowel.

waar.spelling: The 'aa' in 'waar' represents a long /aː/ sound, typical for open syllables.
waar.fast: In connected speech, the /r/ in 'waar is' may be more relaxed or even dropped, leading to a smoother transition between words.

ook.spelling: The long vowel /oː/ is indicated by the open syllable followed by a consonant.
ook.fast: In casual speech, the vowel /oː/ can sometimes become shorter before a following consonant.

zijn.spelling: The diphthong 'ij' in 'zijn' is pronounced as /ɛi/.
zijn.fast: In fast speech, 'zijn' may reduce to a schwa sound, especially in unstressed positions.

nee.spelling: The long vowel /eː/ is represented by the single vowel 'e' in an open syllable.

vriend.fast: In rapid speech, the final /t/ in 'vriend' may be less pronounced or even dropped when followed by a word starting with a consonant.
